open_questions.question: What exact sign-in result and password policy should be used?
open_questions.context: A1: a minimal locally demonstrable sign-in/session flow; no additional policy assumed.

open_questions.question: How should unknown account identifiers be treated under the five-per-account-per-hour limit?
open_questions.context: A4: enforce per known synthetic account; keep public response indistinguishable and do not invent an unknown-account quota.

open_questions.question: What precise presentation and error text should the reset-request and new-password pages use?
open_questions.context: A2: simple server-rendered pages; wireframe appearance is specified only for sign-in.

open_questions.question: How should links be delivered without production notification infrastructure?
open_questions.context: A3: expose them in the in-memory sink for local testing, not in public request responses.

requirements.statement: The sign-in page displays a rectangular outlined card on a white page, headed “Sign in”.
acceptance_criteria: Given a visitor opens the sign-in page, when the page renders, then an outlined rectangular sign-in card with the heading “Sign in” is visible against a white page.

requirements.statement: The sign-in page displays an email input labeled “Email address” with the placeholder `name@example.com`.
acceptance_criteria: Given the sign-in page is open, when its form renders, then the email input has that label and placeholder.

requirements.statement: The sign-in page displays a password input labeled “Password” with masked entry and the wireframe’s `********` placeholder.
acceptance_criteria: Given the sign-in page is open, when the password field renders and a visitor types into it, then the label and placeholder are displayed and entered characters are masked.

requirements.statement: The sign-in page displays a blue, underlined “Forgot password?” link.
acceptance_criteria: Given the sign-in page is open, when the card renders, then the blue underlined link with that exact text is visible.

requirements.statement: The “Forgot password?” link opens the reset-request flow.
acceptance_criteria: Given the sign-in page is open, when the visitor follows the “Forgot password?” link, then a page or form for requesting a reset opens.

requirements.statement: The sign-in card displays a dark “Sign in” button.
acceptance_criteria: Given the sign-in page is open, when the form renders, then a dark button with the text “Sign in” is visible.

requirements.statement: The sign-in page displays the footer “No account? Contact your administrator.”
acceptance_criteria: Given the sign-in page is open, when its footer renders, then this exact text is visible beneath the sign-in form/card.

requirements.statement: A valid synthetic account can sign in and acquire an active session.
acceptance_criteria: Given a configured synthetic account and its current credentials, when its owner submits the sign-in form, then that account has an authenticated active session that can later be invalidated by a reset.

requirements.statement: The reset-request page accepts an account identifier to request a password reset.
acceptance_criteria: Given a visitor has opened the reset-request flow, when the page renders, then the visitor can submit an account email for a reset request.

requirements.statement: A reset request for a known synthetic account issues a usable reset link.
acceptance_criteria: Given a known synthetic account is below the request limit, when its email is submitted for a reset, then a link enabling that account's password-reset flow is issued through the application's in-memory mechanism.

requirements.statement: Reset-request responses do not reveal whether the requested account exists.
acceptance_criteria: Given otherwise equivalent requests for a known account and an unknown identifier, when they are submitted, then the public response is identical, including the displayed message and response outcome; it does not expose existence or a reset link.

requirements.statement: A known account cannot receive more than five reset requests per hour.
acceptance_criteria: Given five reset requests were accepted for one synthetic account during the relevant hour, when a sixth request for that account arrives within that hour, then no additional reset link is issued for it; a request outside that window can be accepted.

requirements.statement: A reset link cannot successfully reset a password more than once.
acceptance_criteria: Given a valid link has completed a reset, when someone attempts a second reset with the same link, then the second reset is rejected without changing the password.

requirements.statement: Reset links expire 30 minutes after issuance.
acceptance_criteria: Given a reset link was issued, when it is submitted at or after 30 minutes from issuance, then the reset is rejected without changing the password.

requirements.statement: Submitting a valid reset link with a new password updates that synthetic account's password.
acceptance_criteria: Given an unexpired, unused reset link for a synthetic account, when the owner completes the reset with a new password, then the account accepts the new password for subsequent sign-in.

requirements.statement: Completing a successful password reset signs the account out of every active session.
acceptance_criteria: Given the account has one or more active sessions, when its password reset completes, then each previously active session is no longer authenticated.

requirements.statement: Every successful reset notifies its account owner.
acceptance_criteria: Given a successful password reset, when the reset completes, then an owner-addressed notification of that reset is recorded; unsuccessful attempts do not count as successful resets.

requirements.statement: The application runs with Python 3.12 and Flask.
acceptance_criteria: Given the documented local application setup uses Python 3.12, when the app is started, then Flask serves the password-reset application.

requirements.statement: The application's sign-in and reset pages are server-rendered.
acceptance_criteria: Given a request for a sign-in or reset page, when Flask handles it, then the response contains the page's rendered form/content from the server rather than depending on a client-rendered application.

requirements.statement: The application uses synthetic accounts rather than real account records.
acceptance_criteria: Given the app is started for local demonstration or tests, when an account is used, then it comes from synthetic account data, with no production identity integration.

requirements.statement: Notifications use an in-memory sink rather than external delivery.
acceptance_criteria: Given a reset-related notification is generated, when it is delivered, then it is inspectable in the in-memory sink and no real delivery service is required.

requirements.statement: Automated pytest tests cover the implemented reset and sign-in requirements.
acceptance_criteria: Given the project is installed for local testing, when pytest is run, then automated tests exercise the sign-in/reset flows, request parity and limit, link single-use and expiry, session invalidation, and owner notification.

requirements.statement: The project documents production limitations.
acceptance_criteria: Given a reader opens the project documentation, when they review the password-reset app's limitations, then they can identify that synthetic accounts and in-memory notifications are demonstration mechanisms and that the app is not production-ready as-is.

requirements.statement: The delivered project contains no deployment or deployment workflow.
acceptance_criteria: Given the delivered repository, when it is inspected, then there are no newly added deployment workflows or instructions to deploy, and the work does not deploy the app.
